steps.say: Saline leads every hypercalcaemia resuscitation, and the exam punishes anyone who reaches for the bisphosphonate first. Zoledronate then lowers calcium over days, not minutes, so severe symptoms need a calcitonin bridge. Diuretics before fluids deepen the very dehydration driving the crisis. Reserve steroids for the lymphoma mechanism described next.
steps.tx: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (cancer driven high calcium) always starts with aggressive isotonic saline (salt water) volume expansion, because calcium induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (kidney water loss) with dehydration. **Zoledronic acid** 4 mg intravenously (a nitrogen bisphosphonate blocking osteoclast bone resorption) follows, acting at 48 hours with its nadir (lowest calcium point) at 4 to 7 days, or denosumab in renal failure. Calcitonin bridges severe cases within 4 to 6 hours but fades by 48 hours, while loop diuretics worsen volume loss and steroids help only calcitriol driven lymphomas.

vis.alt: Bone targeted pharmacology with osteoclast coupling.
vis.caption: Osteoclast coupling with bisphosphonate and denosumab targets. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Half treated hypercalcaemia looks alarming halfway through the course, which tempts premature redosing. Patience wins because the nadir arrives days after the first signs of improvement. Adding denosumab on top of a working bisphosphonate overshoots into dangerous hypocalcaemia. Watchful hydration carries the patient to the nadir safely.
steps.tx: A falling calcium at 48 hours after zoledronic acid means the drug is working toward its 4 to 7 day nadir, so management is continued **hydration** (saline maintenance) with calcium monitoring and no repeat bisphosphonate or added denosumab. Redosing waits at least 7 days, and stacking denosumab now invites severe hypocalcaemia (low calcium) with renal injury. Improving symptoms confirm the bridge is holding, not that therapy failed.

rows: Drug working toward day 4 to 7 nadir

steps.say: Most hypercalcaemia comes from PTHrP, so lymphoma stands apart with its own vitamin D machinery. Tumour macrophages carry the activating enzyme that normal kidneys keep for themselves. That extra renal production explains both the gut absorption pattern and the steroid sensitivity. Examiners test the 80 percent mechanism against this 1 percent one.
steps.tx: Lymphoma hypercalcaemia runs through extrarenal 1 alpha hydroxylase (**CYP27B1**, a vitamin D activating enzyme) in malignant lymphocytes and macrophages, overproducing 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D (**calcitriol**, active vitamin D) that raises gut calcium absorption. Across all cancers, humoral PTHrP (parathyroid hormone related protein) drives 80 percent (squamous, renal, breast), local osteolysis 20 percent, calcitriol about 1 percent and ectopic intact PTH under 1 percent. Calcitonin style physiology explains the steroid response covered next.

vis.alt: PTH calcitriol axis across bone kidney and gut.
vis.caption: PTH and calcitriol control of calcium across bone, kidney and gut. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Steroids pass from useless to essential once calcitriol increases the calcium. Standard prednisone or hydrocortisone doses block the tumour enzyme within days. No bridge cures anything on its own, so parallel cancer therapy decides the final outcome. Matching the drug to the mechanism is the whole exam point.
steps.tx: Calcitriol driven hypercalcaemia answers specifically to **corticosteroids** (prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily or hydrocortisone 200 to 400 mg intravenously daily), which suppress tumour 1 alpha hydroxylase and intestinal absorption. Yet every acute measure from saline to denosumab only bridges, and definitive long term control demands treating the underlying malignancy itself. Steroids fail PTHrP tumours, where bisphosphonates and denosumab lead instead.
